# Oaks Exploratory Data Analysis

For your final project analysis, you have been placed into groups, within which you can collaborate and help each other. Within your group, you will divide up the different data that is available to ask questions. You are required to address TWO questions each.

1.  An ANOVA/GLM question that addresses the impact of the experimental treatments on a measured variable (SPAD, stomatal conductance, or height) in one of the two plant species.
2.  A question of your choice that analyzes one of the abiotic variables (soil moisture, slope, aspect, etc.), past year data, or an interaction within the experiment.

The following worksheet will guide you through developing your research questions, hypotheses, and analysis approach.

### Load your packages

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
```

## Exploratory Data Analysis:

Before you can analyze your specific questions, you need to clean up and get a sense of the data. Exploratory Data Analysis has the following goals:

1.  **Generate questions about your data.**

    1.  [This is not just about your research questions!]{.underline} Questions might include: how many samples are there for each treatment? Why is there a weird outlier in that one variable? Why won't this variable plot?

    2.  More interesting questions might include: Is there a relationship between these variables? Why is there a pattern where one is higher in only that variable?

2.  **Search for answers by visualizing, transforming, and modelling your data.**

    1.  You can identify problems (like outliers or NA values) by plotting data, or transforming and manipulating it. Answers might include: That outlier was entered incorrectly from the original datasheets, OR it keyed to the wrong species; This variable won't plot because R originally read it in as a character instead of a number (and some lines had words entered instead of NA). You can use these answers to

    2.  Visualizing = plotting, transforming = calculating new variables, log transformations, etc. and modelling = fitting linear models/ANOVA tests to the data.

3.  **Use what you learn to refine your questions and/or generate new questions.**

    1.  Let this lead you! Maybe you find a relationship between two variables. Does that mean there is also a relationship with a third variable? Check it out! Today is about looking at EVERYTHING, not just your specific research question.

## Data Cleaning

### How to Examine and Clean Data

In this section we will look at and clean up each of the data sets you identified that you would like to analyze in your research questions. What to look for when data cleaning:

1.  Dimensions
    1.  Does the data have the right number of rows? Are there blank rows of NAs at the bottom that need to be removed?
        - `nrow()`, `dim()`, `glimpse()` to view counts of rows
    2.  Do you have all the columns you need? Do you need to bring in additional information for context?
        - `ncol()`, `str()`, `names()`, `glimpse()` to view column numbers and names
        - `full_join()`, `inner_join()`, `left_join()` etc. to merge with other data based on matching columns
        - Are there columns you won't use that you'd like to exclude for simplicity using `select()`
2.  Column names
    1.  Are your column names tidy (i.e., have no punctuation or spaces, consistent capitals)?
        - `rename()` to fix column names
        - Recommendation: rename some of those messy LICOR columns to more useful and memorable ones!
3.  Data types
    1.  Are your columns in the correct format?
        - `typeof(data$variable)` or `glimpse()` to check column data type
        - `mutate(variable = as.numeric())` to convert to numeric
        - `mutate(variable = as.character())` to convert to string/word
        - `mutate(variable = factor())` to convert to factor
    2.  Do the values in your columns all match the format you want? (e.g., are there characters in a numeric column?
        - `unique(data$variable)` to see all unique values in that column
        - `mutate(variable = case_when([see Data Wrangling demo]))` to repair
    3.  Are there any cells that contain two kinds of information and may need to be separated? (e.g. Tag_Num that also includes sapling A/B or A1, A2, or A3)
        - `separate()` to create two new columns by splitting the data based on a delimiter
4.  Irregular Values
    1.  Do all the values make sense for your data set (e.g., outliers)
        1.  `summary(df$variable)` gives the min & max and other values to see IF there is a weird value
        2.  `which(df$variable == 102.0)` gives the ROW NUMBER of any rows that have that value
        3.  If you find something weird, check it against the original data sheets, correct or remove with `filter()` if appropriate.
        4.  View your data with histograms.

### ANOVA dataset

You may be either examining `SPAD_Data_Raw`, `Height_Data_Raw`, `LICOR_Data_Raw`, or `Moist_Data_Raw` for your ANOVA question. Examine your data set using the diagnostic functions I've given you above in the How to Examine and Clean Data section.

```{r}
Height_Data <- Height_Data_Raw |> 
  #only select alive seedlings for the four treatments mentioned in the instruction.
  filter(
    Dead_Alive == "Alive", 
    Seedling_Ht_cm > 0,
    Treatment %in% c("AC", "DT", "OS","NR")
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    Treatment = factor(Treatment)
    #make a new column for the selected treatments
  )
Height_Data |> 
  count(Treatment)
#check how many alive seedlings are in each group

Height_Data |> 
  count(Block, Tag_Num, Sapling_AB_etc) |> 
  filter(n > 1)
#make sure no duplicated individuals

Height_Data
```

```{r}
ggplot(Height_Data) +
  aes(x = Treatment, y = Seedling_Ht_cm) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Seedling Height Across Habitat Treatments",
    x = "Treatment",
    y = "Seedling Height (cm)"
  ) 
```

```{r}
#one-way ANOVA
Height_ANOVA <- aov(Seedling_Ht_cm ~ Treatment, data = Height_Data)
summary(Height_ANOVA)
#plot of Residuals vs. Fitted values. Homogeneity of variance
plot(Height_ANOVA, which = 1)
#Q-Q plot for normailty
plot(Height_ANOVA, which = 2)

#Shapiro-Wilk test for testing normality. Very small p-value, indicating not normally distributed
shapiro.test(Height_ANOVA$residuals)

# Bartlett Test of Homogeneity of Variances
bartlett.test(Seedling_Ht_cm ~ Treatment, data = Height_Data)

#Thukey post hoc test for results between each treatment
TukeyHSD(Height_ANOVA)

##I performed a one-way ANOVA to examine differences in seedling height among the four treatments. However, the Shapiro-Wilk test and Q-Q plot suggested that the residuals deviated from normality. Bartlett's test also indicated unequal variances among treatments. Therefore, the assumptions of a standard one-way ANOVA may not be fully met, and the results should be interpreted with caution.
```

```{r}
#curious about the number of dead seedlings for each groups
Height_Death <- Height_Data_Raw |> 
  #only select dead seedlings for the four treatments mentioned in the instruction.
  filter(
    Dead_Alive == "Dead", 
    Seedling_Ht_cm == 0,
    Treatment %in% c("AC", "DT", "OS","NR"),
    !is.na(Dead_Alive)
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    Treatment = factor(Treatment)
    #make a new column for the selected treatments
  )

Height_Death |> 
  count(Treatment)
#check how many dead seedlings are in each group

Height_Death

#count number of dead or alive seedlings for each treatment
Death_Alive <- Height_Data_Raw |>
  filter(Treatment %in% c("AC", "DT", "OS", "NR"),
         !is.na(Dead_Alive)) |>
  count(Treatment, Dead_Alive)

Death_Alive
```

### Regression dataset

Repeat the steps you took for your ANOVA data for your second data set of choice/

```{r}
# View data set

# check relevant columns
LICOR_Data_Raw |>
  select(contains("gsw")) |>
  summary()

Moist_Data_Raw |>
  select(contains("VWC")) |>
  summary()
```

```{r}
# Inspect soil moisture records
Moist_Data_Raw |>
  select(Date, Block, Treatment,
         VWC1_perc, VWC2_perc, VWC3_perc)
```

```{r}
#clean soil moisture data
Moist_Data <- Moist_Data_Raw |>
  mutate(
    #convert to numerical 
    VWC1_perc = as.numeric(VWC1_perc),
    VWC2_perc = as.numeric(VWC2_perc),
    VWC3_perc = as.numeric(VWC3_perc)
  ) |>
  #remove "NA"
  filter(!is.na(VWC1_perc),
         !is.na(VWC2_perc),
         !is.na(VWC3_perc)) |>
  mutate(
    #calculate mean between VWC1_perc, VWC2_perc, VWC3_perc
    VWC = rowMeans(
      across(c(VWC1_perc, VWC2_perc, VWC3_perc))
    )
  )


Moist_Data
#inspect soil moisture
summary(Moist_Data$VWC)
nrow(Moist_Data)
```

```{r}
#number of unique block + treatment combinations
Moist_Data |>
  count(Block, Treatment) |>
  nrow()

Height_Data |>
  count(Block, Treatment) |>
  nrow()

#average seedling height for each block + treatment
Height_Summary <- Height_Data |>
  group_by(Block, Treatment) |>
  summarise(
    Mean_Height = mean(Seedling_Ht_cm, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
Height_Summary
# average soil moisture for each block + treatment
Moist_Summary <- Moist_Data |>
  group_by(Block, Treatment) |>
  summarise(
    Mean_VWC = mean(VWC, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
Moist_Summary
# match the two datasets
Oak_Regression <- inner_join(
  Moist_Summary,
  Height_Summary,
  by = c("Block", "Treatment")
)

# check the number of matched observations
nrow(Oak_Regression)

```

```{r}
Oak_LM <- lm(Mean_Height ~ Mean_VWC, data = Oak_Regression)
summary(Oak_LM)

#A linear regression was used to examine the relationship between mean soil moisture and mean seedling height across 18 Block-Treatment combinations. The relationship was negative but not statistically significant (F = 1.36, p = 0.260, R-squared = 0.078). Mean soil moisture explained approximately 7.8% of the variation in mean seedling height. Therefore, there is no linear relationship between the two variables.
```

## Exploratory Data Analysis

Now that your data is (probably, mostly!) clean, it is time to explore your data! Feel free to explore not just the variables/data set relevant to your research question, but to explore variables your teammates are examining as well. Use this space to generate more questions, identify if there are more things to fix in your data cleaning, etc.

Not sure where to start?

- Make a histogram of each variable and write down your observations

- Plot variables against each other to explore relationships (boxplots and scatterplots are a good starting point)

- Use facet_grid to explore different groupings of data

**There are no wrong answers! If you make 3+ graphs and show you're thinking critically about them, you will get full credit for this assignment.**

Go for it!

```{r}
ggplot(Height_Data) +
  aes(x = Treatment, y = Seedling_Ht_cm) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(
    title = "Seedling Height Across Habitat Treatments",
    x = "Treatment",
    y = "Seedling Height (cm)"
  )
```

```{r}
ggplot(Death_Alive) +
  aes(x = Treatment, y = n, fill = Dead_Alive) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  labs(
    title = "Seedling Survival Across Habitat Treatments",
    x = "Treatment",
    y = "Proportion",
    fill = "Survival Status"
  ) 
#porpotion of alive and dead seedlings for each treatment
```

```{r}
ggplot(Oak_Regression, aes(x = Mean_VWC, y = Mean_Height)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  geom_text(x = 14, y = 60,
            #position of the label for regression equation and Rsq)
            label = paste(
              "R-squared =", round(summary(Oak_LM)$r.squared, 3),
              "\ny =", round(coef(Oak_LM)[2],3),
              #change to a new line for "y =" & "x + "
              "x +", round(coef(Oak_LM)[1], 3)))+
  labs(
    x = "Mean Soil Moisture (VWC, %)",
    y = "Mean Seedling Height (cm)",
    title = "Soil Moisture vs. Seedling Height"
  ) 
```
